block_text_edits.old: Opportunity cost is often illustrated with a production possibility curve (PPC). The curve shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently used. Moving along the curve shows opportunity cost: if an economy moves from 100 tonnes of maize and 40 cattle to 120 tonnes of maize and 30 cattle, the opportunity cost of the extra 20 tonnes of maize is the 10 cattle given up. A point inside the curve shows that some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently. A point outside the curve cannot be reached with present resources and technology.

block.heading: Drawing a production possibility curve
block.text:
Opportunity cost can be illustrated with a production possibility curve (PPC). The curve shows the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently used, with resources and technology fixed. Suppose a farming district can use its land, labour and equipment to produce maize and cattle. Its yearly production schedule is: A, 0 t of maize and 80 cattle; B, 50 t and 75 cattle; C, 100 t and 60 cattle; D, 150 t and 35 cattle; E, 200 t and no cattle. Put maize (tonnes per year) on the horizontal axis and cattle (head per year) on the vertical axis, plot the five combinations and join them with a smooth curve.

![Production possibility curve for the farming district, with point J inside it, point K outside it and the movement from C to D](diagrams/item-6145-1.1-011-proc-answer.png)

Moving along the curve shows opportunity cost. From C to D the district gains 50 t of maize and gives up 25 cattle, so the opportunity cost of the extra 50 t of maize is 25 cattle. From B to C the same 50 t of maize cost only 15 cattle. The cost rises because the land and workers moved into maize last are better suited to raising cattle, which is why this curve is bowed outwards. If resources were equally suited to both goods, the PPC would be a straight line and each extra 50 t of maize would cost the same number of cattle.

Point J (50 t of maize and 40 cattle) lies inside the curve. Some resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, because the district could raise 75 cattle alongside the same 50 t of maize. Point K (100 t of maize and 80 cattle) lies outside the curve and cannot be reached with present resources and technology. More resources or better technology could shift the whole curve outwards.

item.prompt: A farming district fully and efficiently uses its fixed land, labour and equipment to produce maize and cattle. Its yearly production schedule is A (0 t maize, 80 cattle), B (50 t, 75), C (100 t, 60), D (150 t, 35) and E (200 t, 0). Use the schedule to draw the district's production possibility curve (PPC), with maize on the horizontal axis. Plot J (50 t, 40 cattle) and K (100 t, 80 cattle) and state what each shows. Show the change from C to D and state its opportunity cost (4).
item.canonical_answer: Plot A (0, 80), B (50, 75), C (100, 60), D (150, 35) and E (200, 0), with maize (tonnes per year) on the horizontal axis and cattle (head per year) on the vertical axis, and join them with a smooth curve bowed outwards: this is the PPC. J (50, 40) lies inside the curve: resources are unemployed or used inefficiently, because 50 t of maize could be produced alongside 75 cattle. K (100, 80) lies outside the curve: it cannot be reached with the district's present resources and technology. Moving from C to D gives 50 t more maize (an arrow across from C) and 25 fewer cattle (an arrow down to D), so the opportunity cost of the extra 50 t of maize is 25 cattle. From B to C the same 50 t cost only 15 cattle; the cost rises because land and workers better suited to cattle are moved into maize.
